title: Moneton
summary: The Moneton, the “Big Water” people, lived along the Kanawha and New rivers on Kentucky’s eastern approaches when English explorers noted them in 1671.
bodyMarkdown:
The Moneton were a Native nation of the Kanawha Valley in present West Virginia, east of Kentucky. English colonists wrote about them only briefly in the 1670s, and then they disappear from the record. Their story shows how little is known about the Ohio Valley's peoples on the eve of European contact.

## Homeland and name

In the late 1600s they [lived in the Kanawha Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moneton) near the Kanawha and New rivers. Their name translates to "Big Water" people. Their towns lay west of the Manahoac and Tutelo nations.

## First written mentions

The Moneton enter the written record through Virginia expeditions sponsored by the trader Abraham Wood. The first mention of them came from Thomas Batts in 1671. On the [Batts and Fallam expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batts_and_Fallam_expedition), Batts, Thomas Wood and Robert Fallam set out on September 1, 1671, from near present Petersburg, Virginia. Their commission was to find "the ebbing and flowing of the water behind the mountains," and they are credited with reaching the New River, long called Wood's River.

In 1674 Abraham Wood sent his servant Gabriel Arthur from Fort Henry, near Appomattox, to visit tribes and expand the fur trade. The Moneton capital was described as "a great town." Arthur [lived among the Tomahitans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Wood) for almost a year and traveled with them as far north as the Ohio River. That 1674 account is the last contemporary mention of the Moneton.

## Who were they?

The Moneton may have belonged to the [Fort Ancient culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fort_Ancient), which flourished from about 1000 to 1750 CE in the Ohio Valley, including northern Kentucky and western West Virginia. Their language was never recorded. Some scholars think it was Siouan, related to Tutelo and Ofo, while others argue it was Algonquian, pointing to ties with Fort Ancient peoples such as the Shawnee.

## What happened to them

The Moneton were likely forced to merge with other nations in the Virginia Piedmont because of colonialism. The ethnohistorian Isaac J. Emrick argues that they probably joined the Shawnee in the 1600s.

That fits the wider picture. The Fort Ancient culture [declined](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fort_Ancient) in the 1600s, likely from introduced diseases, warfare and environmental change. Smallpox and other diseases may have spread through Native trade networks before Europeans arrived in person. By the 1700s no Fort Ancient villages were still occupied, and some people may have joined Algonquian-speaking groups such as the Shawnee, though direct links remain uncertain.

## Kentucky today

The Moneton lived east of Kentucky, but their history is part of the story of the upper Ohio Valley before Kentucky's pioneer stations. Neighboring peoples of the same era are told in [Mosopelea (Ofo) and the Ohio Valley](/stories/mosopelea-ofo-the-ohio-valley/) and [Hardin Village](/stories/hardin-village-15gp22/).
